column2: Emigrant Government North of the Vaal
A small emigrant community held together by wagons, grazing claims and local commandos rather than a mature state bureaucracy.
The settlement on the Vet River is governed through public meetings, field-cornets and the authority of local commandants.
A young emigrant settlement is beginning to turn scattered farms into a more permanent political centre.
The Thirty-Three Articles give the linked Winburg and Potchefstroom communities a common legal framework without erasing strong regional loyalties.
British annexation south of the Vaal has severed the Winburg districts from the northern emigrant government.
Britain has formally renounced authority over the emigrant farmers north of the Vaal River.
Distance, local commandants and a frontier economy give the northern district an unusually independent political character.
Rival claims to executive and military authority have divided the republic and armed burghers are choosing sides.
A new election and negotiated settlement are slowly restoring common authority after the factional conflict.
Regional delegates are attempting to turn scattered emigrant communities into a more permanent authority north of the Vaal.
The eastern community has asserted a distinct republican government while maintaining close ties to the wider Transvaal political world.
The Buffalo River settlers have converted their local community into a small frontier republic.

Louis Tregardt and Hans van Rensburg have led small parties of emigrant farmers into the far northern interior. Their wagons are few, their authority informal, and African communities remain the dominant political presence in the region. Yet for a time the trekkers have established a separate camp near the Soutpansberg, beyond the effective reach of the Cape.
Let the distant trekkers fend for themselves.
No separate settler authority will be tolerated.

The first pioneer encampment did not endure, but in 1848 followers of Andries Hendrik Potgieter have returned north and founded a permanent settlement near the Soutpansberg. The new community is already developing its own commandant, landdrost and frontier institutions, while relations with Venda communities remain tense and contested.

Voortrekker families are concentrating around the Vet River country. The settlement later known as Winburg is still more a political community than a finished town, but meetings of burghers and local commandants are beginning to give the emigrants a territorial identity of their own.

After agreements over land and the defeat of Mzilikazi's power on the Highveld, Andries Hendrik Potgieter's followers are establishing themselves around the Mooi River. A permanent town is beginning to take shape and the emigrants are proclaiming their independence from colonial authority.
The settlement has become more than a wagon camp. Farms, streets and public offices are taking shape around Potchefstroom, giving the western Transvaal its first durable administrative centre.
A republic needs a seat of government.

Representatives of the emigrant communities have met at Potchefstroom and adopted thirty-three articles regulating government and justice. Winburg and Potchefstroom are increasingly being treated as parts of one political system, even though local loyalties remain strong and no settled official name has yet been adopted.
Unite the emigrant communities under the Articles.

Sir Harry Smith has proclaimed British sovereignty over the country between the Orange and Vaal rivers. Accepting the proclamation will cut Winburg away from the northern emigrant government. Resistance would mean confronting imperial troops on the Highveld.

Delegates from the scattered Transvaal communities have met at Derdepoort to create a more permanent Volksraad and executive authority for the emigrants north of the Vaal. Regional commandants remain powerful, but the idea of a common state is taking firmer shape.

British commissioners have met representatives of the emigrant farmers north of the Vaal. Recognition would remove a troublesome frontier commitment and acknowledge their right to govern themselves, while preserving British interests south of the river.
Recognise the emigrant farmers north of the Vaal.
Britain will not abandon its claims.

The Sand River Convention of 17 January 1852 recognises the independence of the emigrant communities north of the Vaal. Potchefstroom now continues as the Transvaal republic. Its institutions and the formal South African Republic name develop further in the following years.
Continue as the independent Transvaal republic.

Sand River recognition has already secured the independence of the northern communities. Potchefstroom now continues under the Transvaal republic administration, preserving our territory, armed forces and government records.
The districts are not ready for one name.

The eastern settlers who moved away from unhealthy Ohrigstad have developed a strong local identity. Their leaders now insist that Lydenburg should govern itself as a republic rather than submit to the growing central authority in the western Transvaal.
Let Lydenburg stand on its own.

The Buffalo River settlers have turned their grazing settlement into a recognised local government. Agreements with Mpande, disputed boundaries and pressure from neighbouring states have encouraged the community to formalise its own republican institutions.
A small republic on the Buffalo River.

The northern commandants have agreed in principle to join the wider South African Republic. Distance and strong local institutions make immediate absorption difficult, so the settlement is likely to retain substantial autonomy even while acknowledging the common republican government.
Join the republic while retaining local autonomy.

The administration of Zoutpansberg has marked its association with the South African Republic with a public celebration at Schoemansdal. The northern district keeps its own commandants, magistrates and local institutions, while acknowledging the SAR as the centre of a wider republican union. Pretoria's representatives promise that this arrangement will bring practical cooperation in trade, roads and frontier defence without erasing Zoutpansberg's local government. The compact is a union of governments under one republican protection, not the disappearance of the northern community.
Fund shared roads, supply stores and district administration.
Celebrate the compact without new commitments.

The administration of Zoutpansberg has celebrated its association with the South African Republic. The compact places the northern republic under SAR protection while leaving its local institutions and government in place. The two administrations intend to cooperate on roads, supplies and frontier defence, and the agreement is expected to strengthen both communities until their political differences return to the fore.

Zoutpansberg's administration has celebrated its new association with the South African Republic. The northern district retains its local government under SAR protection, and both administrations are preparing a period of closer cooperation.
Zoutpansberg has entered a celebrated compact under South African Republic protection while retaining local government.

A five-year programme of shared administration, frontier supplies and agricultural development links Zoutpansberg with the South African Republic. The compact ends when the 1862 civil-war crisis begins.

The contest over executive authority has become a constitutional crisis. Stephanus Schoeman and his supporters reject the decisions of their opponents, while Paul Kruger and the Volksraad insist that no commandant may place himself above the law. Armed burghers are beginning to gather behind rival leaders.
The Volksraad will enforce its authority.

The northern faction has rejected the authority of the central government. Supporters of Stephanus Schoeman and allied commandants are mobilising in Zoutpansberg and the western districts, turning a dispute over office into an armed struggle for control of the republic.
An Armistice Beneath the Karee Trees

After years of factional skirmishing, neither side can claim that republican government has benefited from the conflict. The opposing commandos are prepared to accept an armistice, submit the dispute to constitutional procedures and hold a fresh presidential election.
End the civil war and call a new election.
There can be no settlement yet.

Years of negotiation have brought Zoutpansberg increasingly within the institutions of the South African Republic. The question is no longer whether the northern settlers belong to the wider republican system, but how much separate authority their district should retain.

Conflict with Venda communities has made the northern settlement increasingly untenable. A republican force cannot secure the surrounding mountains, and the settlers at Schoemansdal are preparing to abandon the town rather than remain exposed on an isolated frontier.
The commandos will hold the north.
